title: Joshua 12:1–6
context: Chapter 12 begins a list of the kings Israel defeated, starting east of the Jordan. Under Moses, Israel defeated Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled from Heshbon, and Og king of Bashan, described as one of the remnant of the Rephaim (Numbers 21:21–35; Deuteronomy 2:26–3:11). Moses gave their land to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (Numbers 32). Places such as Heshbon, the Arnon, the Jabbok, and the Salt Sea are widely identified east of the Jordan and around the Dead Sea, though some boundary details are uncertain. Both traditions read the list as remembrance: God’s faithfulness under Moses is recorded alongside his faithfulness under Joshua, so that one story of promise and fulfillment spans both leaders.

verses.text: Now these are the kings of the land, whom the children of Israel struck, and possessed their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, and all the Arabah eastward:
verses.arminianNotes:
These are the kings whom Israel defeated east of the Jordan, from the Arnon valley to Mount Hermon and all the eastern Arabah. The list begins with Moses’ victories.

Arminian readers note that the list invites remembrance: Israel must not forget what God has done, because forgetting leads to unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the record unites the work of Moses and Joshua into one story of God’s faithfulness. The conquest began before the Jordan was crossed.

Both traditions read the list as a testimony that God’s promises are fulfilled in real places and real history.

verses.text: Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and the middle of the valley, and half Gilead, even to the river Jabbok, the border of the children of Ammon;
verses.arminianNotes:
Sihon king of the Amorites ruled from Heshbon, from Aroer on the Arnon to the Jabbok, the border of Ammon. His defeat is recounted in Numbers 21:21–31.

Arminian readers note that Sihon refused Israel’s request for peaceful passage, a choice that led to his defeat.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Deuteronomy 2:30 says the LORD hardened Sihon’s spirit so that he would be delivered into Israel’s hand, a parallel to Joshua 11:20.

Both traditions read Sihon’s defeat as an early sign of God’s faithfulness, later celebrated in Psalm 136:19.

verses.text: and the Arabah to the sea of Chinneroth, eastward, and to the sea of the Arabah, even the Salt Sea, eastward, the way to Beth Jeshimoth; and on the south, under the slopes of Pisgah:
verses.arminianNotes:
Sihon’s territory included the Arabah to the sea of Chinneroth and the Salt Sea, toward Beth Jeshimoth and under the slopes of Pisgah. The region is described in detail.

Arminian readers note that the land east of the Jordan was given as a real inheritance, not merely a stopping place on the way.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Pisgah is where Moses viewed the promised land before his death (Deuteronomy 34:1). God’s purposes for Moses ended in grace.

Both traditions treat the boundary details cautiously while affirming that God gave this land to his people.

verses.text: and the border of Og king of Bashan, of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei,
verses.arminianNotes:
Og king of Bashan, of the remnant of the Rephaim, lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei. Deuteronomy 3:11 recalls his great bed of iron.

Arminian readers note that Og, like the Anakim, represented the kind of power that frightened Israel, yet he was defeated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Rephaim are presented as a people of great stature, and God’s victory over their remnant displays his power over every threat.

Both traditions avoid speculation about the Rephaim beyond what Scripture says and draw comfort from God’s victory.

verses.text: and ruled in Mount Hermon, and in Salecah, and in all Bashan, to the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and half Gilead, the border of Sihon king of Heshbon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Og ruled in Mount Hermon, Salecah, and all Bashan, to the Geshurites and Maacathites and half of Gilead. His realm was large.

Arminian readers note that the Geshurites and Maacathites were not driven out (Joshua 13:13), another sign that possession was incomplete.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the defeat of Og, together with Sihon, became a lasting memory of God’s power in Israel’s worship (compare Psalm 135:11).

Both traditions read the verse as part of the record of God’s faithfulness, honest about what remained unfinished.

verses.text: Moses the servant of the LORD and the children of Israel struck them. Moses the servant of the LORD gave it for a possession to the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses and Israel struck these kings, and Moses gave their land to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. The eastern tribes received their inheritance first.

Arminian readers note that these tribes asked for the land and accepted obligations to help their brothers (Numbers 32), which they fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the title Moses the servant of the LORD appears twice, stressing that his work was done under God’s authority.

Both traditions see continuity between Moses’ leadership and Joshua’s, both serving one purpose under God.
